title: Two Halves, One Volume
subtitle: Module 10 — claim, class and volume, the CSI split, and why storage decides where a Pod can run

meta.note: Timing comes from the synthesised audio. estSeconds is a planning estimate only. Content authority: assets/content.js unit u10.

beats.title: You are here
beats.narration: A Pod is scheduled and stuck, and the events point at four different components. This is the CSI segment of the request path. It covers the three objects that describe storage, and the two halves of a driver that deliver it. It covers the handshake that decides where a Pod can run. By the end you can say which half of the driver failed, and where its evidence lives.

visual.spec: REUSE spineLocator with the CSI segment lit.

beats.title: Claim, class, volume
beats.narration: Three objects, three different jobs. A PVC is a namespaced request for storage, and it names size, access mode and class. A PV is cluster-scoped capacity with a reclaim policy. A StorageClass is the recipe: how to provision, and when to bind. Access mode and reclaim policy are part of that contract, not optional detail.

visual.spec: NEW. Three objects side by side, each labelled with its scope, which is the distinction people get wrong: PVC inside a namespace boundary; PV and StorageClass outside it, cluster-scoped. Draw the namespace boundary explicitly as a container so the PVC sits visibly inside it and the other two visibly outside. Under each, one line on its job.

beats.title: Pending on purpose
beats.narration: A PVC using WaitForFirstConsumer sits Pending with no Pod referencing it. That is not a bug. The binding mode exists so storage is created in a zone the Pod can actually be scheduled into. Pending is the designed state. Bind it early instead and you can end up with a volume in a zone that has no room for the Pod that needs it.

visual.spec: NEW. Two zones with different spare capacity. Immediate binding: the volume is created in zone A, then the Pod cannot be scheduled there and is stuck — a volume and a Pod in different places, both valid, together useless. WaitForFirstConsumer: the claim visibly waits, the Pod is scheduled to zone B, and only then is the volume created, in zone B. Label the waiting state as designed, not failed.

beats.title: Four reasons, four checks
beats.narration: When a claim really is stuck, the evidence has to distinguish causes. Is it waiting deliberately, because nothing consumes it yet. Is there no capacity. Was it rejected by quota. Or is there no topologically compatible node. Those are four different problems with four different fixes, and the replica count of your workload tells you nothing about any of them.

visual.spec: NEW. One Pending PVC at the top, four candidate causes fanning out beneath it, each with the specific evidence that confirms or eliminates it. Set a discarded non-signal apart — replica count — struck through, because reaching for it is the common mistake. Give each cause its distinguishing check at full type scale.

beats.title: The split people merge
beats.narration: CSI has two halves that people merge into one. On the control-plane side, sidecars watch Kubernetes objects and call CSI Controller RPCs. The common pair is external-provisioner and external-attacher. external-resizer and external-snapshotter join only when those features are installed. On the node side, a privileged plugin runs the node RPCs so the kubelet can mount into the container. The two halves never call each other. They meet through API objects, the PV and the VolumeAttachment.

visual.spec: NEW. Two clearly separated halves with no direct arrow between them — that absence is the point. Left, control plane: the four named sidecars watching objects and calling Controller RPCs. Right, node: the privileged plugin running stage and publish. Between them, drawn as the only connection, the API objects they both touch: PV and VolumeAttachment. Name all four sidecars legibly.

beats.title: Only one half is privileged
beats.narration: Only one of those halves has to be privileged and present on every node. Mounting is a node-local privileged operation. The controller half talks to the storage provider's API and can run anywhere the control plane runs. So a controller-side failure and a node-side failure look nothing alike.

visual.spec: NEW. The node half drawn on every node, marked privileged; the controller half drawn once, anywhere in the control plane, unprivileged. Then the two failure signatures side by side: controller-side (nothing provisions, no PV appears at all) versus node-side (PV exists and attaches, the Pod still cannot mount). The contrast in symptom is the takeaway.

beats.title: Claim to container, in order
beats.narration: End to end, the path has ordered stages, not one fixed sequence. The claim is created. Under Immediate binding, the provisioner creates the volume and the PV binds. Under WaitForFirstConsumer, the scheduler picks topology first, and the provisioner then creates the volume there. Once a node is known, the attach-detach controller creates a VolumeAttachment, and the external-attacher calls ControllerPublishVolume. The node plugin may stage the volume, then publishes it into the Pod's path. Only then does the kubelet start the containers that need that mount.

visual.spec: NEW. The six steps as one continuous journey filling the stage width: claim created → provisioner creates the volume → attacher attaches, VolumeAttachment recorded → NodeStageVolume on the node → NodePublishVolume into the Pod's target path → container starts. Show the object each step produces beneath it, and mark which side of the CSI split each step belongs to by colour, so the control-plane half and the node half are visible as regions of the same journey. CORRECTION: the attach-detach controller creates the VolumeAttachment; the external-attacher watches it and calls ControllerPublishVolume. Do not draw the attacher creating the object, and do not draw provisioning as always preceding scheduler involvement — that is Immediate binding only.

beats.title: Stage once, publish per Pod
beats.narration: The node half can have two steps, and the difference matters. When the driver supports staging, NodeStageVolume runs once per volume per node and makes the device usable there. NodePublishVolume then runs per Pod target path and bind-mounts into the container. If the driver has no stage capability, only publish runs. Knowing which call failed tells you whether you are debugging the device or the bind mount.

visual.spec: NEW. One node, one staged device, and two Pods each getting their own publish into their own target path. Show stage occurring exactly once while publish occurs per Pod. Then fail each independently: a stage failure leaves no usable device at all; a publish failure leaves a healthy staged device that never reaches one container. Two different logs, labelled. CORRECTION: staging is optional (STAGE_UNSTAGE_VOLUME). Show the no-stage driver going straight to publish. Stage is once per volume per node, not once per node overall.

beats.title: Storage is not a later phase
beats.narration: With WaitForFirstConsumer, storage is not a later phase after a blind schedule. The scheduler selects a node using the Pod's constraints and the driver's topology signals. Only then does the provisioner create the volume in that topology. If no node can satisfy both compute and storage topology, the Pod simply stays unschedulable.

visual.spec: NEW. Scheduler and provisioner facing each other, each visibly waiting on the other, with the zone constraint between them. Show the deadlock read as a negotiation rather than a bug: each is waiting for information only the other has, and the binding mode is what breaks the tie. Then resolve it — zone agreed, Pod placed, volume created there. CORRECTION: this is not a mutual standoff. The scheduler selects topology first, then the provisioner creates the volume there. Do not draw each side waiting on the other.

beats.title: Scheduled, and stuck mounting
beats.narration: A Pod is scheduled and stuck mounting. There is an order. Check the VolumeAttachment first — did attach succeed at all. Then the CSI sidecar logs on the control-plane side. Then whether the node plugin registered on that node, and its logs. Then the kubelet's logs for stage and publish errors. Then credentials, device state, filesystem, and multi-attach constraints.

visual.spec: NEW. An ordered trace, each step lighting as named, with the artefact you actually inspect beside it — the VolumeAttachment object, the sidecar log, the node plugin registration, the kubelet log, then the device-level checks. Emphasise step one: the VolumeAttachment splits control-plane problems from node problems in a single check. Rows that wrap; do not clip the longer checks.

beats.title: Back to the spine
beats.narration: The CSI segment, then. A storage failure can block scheduling before a Pod has a node, or block setup after binding. First check whether the claim is bound and whether the Pod has a node name. Then decide whether the failed step is an object update, an RPC, or a mount. Read the events and the log that owns that step.

visual.spec: REUSE, reversed: the CSI segment shrinks back into the spine. Module order follows the course rather than the packet path, so do not light an adjacent segment — hold the spine whole and let the module counter advance to eleven.
